Can you understand pain you’ve never felt? Many of us assume empathy means reliving another’s exact hurt. In practice, understanding often works by building a model: we use language, analogy and what we already know about suffering to make sense of someone else’s state. A clinician, for example, may never have lived with chronic illness yet can still recognise the structural features of that patient's distress—relentlessness, loss of agency, social isolation—by listening and drawing on clinical knowledge.

But beware a common trap: imagining another’s feelings too quickly imports your own assumptions. Neurobiology suggests our brains respond to salience and aversiveness generally, not to a bespoke “pain replay.” And culturally different expressions of distress can mislead even generous listeners—what looks calm to one observer may signal deep suffering in another cultural idiom.

So the wiser strategy is iterative: listen, test your interpretation, revise. Empathy works best as a corrective practice rather than a confident claim. How might you change your approach next time you encounter suffering that feels unfamiliar?

Can you understand pain you’ve never felt? That tension—between belief in empathy’s reach and the worry that we merely project ourselves onto others—matters for clinicians, carers and anyone who encounters suffering.

Humans do not need identical sensory replay to construct a useful understanding of another’s pain. Cognitive abstraction, analogy and semantic knowledge allow us to map structural features of distress (loss, exhaustion, erosion of agency) onto our own baseline. A clinician without chronic illness, for example, can form an effective model of a chronic patient’s reality through attentive listening, clinical knowledge and careful analogy.

Yet we must preserve an important limitation. Some interpretations of neuroscience caution that overlapping brain responses may reflect general salience or aversiveness rather than an exact replay of another person’s sensations. Combined with the emotional egocentricity bias—our tendency to project our expressive norms onto others—this means empathy often produces an interpretive approximation rather than a direct replication of another’s subjective pain.

Given that, the practical takeaway is epistemic humility: treat your initial empathy as a provisional hypothesis. Listen, revise and test your interpretations instead of assuming you already know what the other person feels. How will you hold that humility next time you try to understand someone whose suffering you have not lived?
